sections.html:
Grand Forks is the Grand Forks County seat. It lies on the west bank of the Red River of the North, at the point where the Red Lake River joins it. About 29.3 square miles sit at roughly 837 feet of elevation. Across the water is East Grand Forks, Minnesota, and the two cities together form a metro area of 104,184 people. Sellers on this side follow North Dakota rules and deal with Grand Forks County offices, while sellers in East Grand Forks follow Minnesota rules.

The city counted 59,166 residents in 2020, up 12.0 percent from 52,838 in 2010. The median age is 30.2, which fits a university and military town. Rentals and student turnover are a fact of life for owners here, and many sales follow a tenant move or a job change.

The 1997 Red River flood did more damage in Grand Forks than in any other major valley city that year, and a downtown fire destroyed 11 buildings at the peak. Peak flow reached about 135,000 cubic feet per second.

The city's response reshaped neighborhoods. Voluntary buyouts in 1997 and 1998 covered 850 properties. Crews demolished 694 dwellings and moved 161 houses. An English Coulee diversion channel of 9.5 miles and 12 new pump stations were built, and the project across Grand Forks and East Grand Forks cost $409 million. Levee tops are about 10 feet wide, and floodwalls add 3 feet. The city says the system could handle a 500-year flood by adding clay to the levees. Roughly 20 miles of greenway trails and a golf course now fill the old floodplain.

For a seller, the practical point is to know where the lot sits relative to the levees, since buyers ask. A tight building envelope, a sound roof and a working furnace also count for more here than in a milder place, because average snowfall is 48.4 inches and January highs average 15.8 degrees Fahrenheit.

Two governments split the work. The City of Grand Forks Assessing Department values property inside the city, and the Grand Forks County Treasurer sends the bill and collects the money. The assessing office also appraises new construction each year and checks exemption and credit claims.

City inspections run on a six-year cycle, so about one-sixth of properties are visited each year. Owners may decline an interior inspection, in which case the office judges from the outside. The assessing office is at City Hall, 255 N 4th Street, and its email is GFAssessing@grandforksgov.com.

Statements are mailed by December 26. The tax is due January 1 and carries no penalty until March 1. Pay the full year by February 15 and you earn a 5 percent discount.

DateRule under N.D.C.C. 57-20-01
February 155% discount if the full year is paid
March 1First installment due; 3% penalty after
May 1Additional 3%
July 1Additional 3%
October 15Second installment due; first-installment penalty grows by 3%; second installment carries 6% after

Send mail to the county treasurer at PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638, or call 701-780-8292. Balances can be looked up online through the county's Tyler iTax and Vanguard property search pages.

A special assessment spreads the cost of an infrastructure project across the properties that benefit from it. The city says these are not property taxes. They can pay for sidewalks, street paving and lighting, water main, storm sewer, sanitary sewer and flood protection.

Repayment terms depend on the project type:

  • Water mains, sanitary sewer and storm sewer: 25 years
  • Paving, asphalt or concrete: 25 years
  • Street lighting, sidewalks and flood control: 20 years
  • Gravel or maintenance streets: 5 to 10 years

Questions go to the city's Finance and Administrative Services Department, 255 N 4th Street, 701-746-2671. Ask for the remaining balance before you list, because buyers and lenders will want a payoff figure.

Start with the city. State law requires a city Board of Equalization meeting, and an appeal by letter, phone or electronic message counts as appearing in person. Written appeals can go to PO Box 5200, Grand Forks ND 58206.

  • City board: first 15 days of April
  • County board: first 10 days of June
  • State board: second Tuesday in August, and only if you appeared at the city and county boards
  • Abatement: by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes payable

Before the April meeting, collect comparable sales, an appraisal or repair bids. Evidence beats opinion at every one of these boards.

Unpaid property tax does not block a sale. The title company pays the county from your proceeds at closing, so ask for a payoff figure that includes special assessments and penalties.

Deeds are recorded at the Grand Forks County Recorder's Office, 151 South 4th Street, phone 701-780-8262. North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax, and the office accepts electronic recording through Simplifile, CSC Recording Solutions, Indecomm and ePN.

A county can foreclose a tax lien after taxes go unpaid into the third year, and an owner can stop it by paying everything owed by October 1. The county website posts a Notice of Foreclosure of Tax Lien each year.

If you are behind, selling before that notice arrives keeps your options open. A sensible order of work:

  • Call the Treasurer for the tax payoff and the city for special assessments.
  • Gather your mortgage payoff letter, if there is a loan.
  • Pick a closing date ahead of the next penalty step.
  • Have the title company confirm every payoff in writing.

We buy Grand Forks houses as they are, and the title company handles the county payoff at closing.

sections.h2: What the county and city each want from a seller
sections.html:
A Grand Forks sale touches two sets of offices, and knowing which one answers which question saves phone calls. The county Treasurer, at 701-780-8292, knows the real estate tax balance and whether anything is delinquent. The city's Finance and Administrative Services Department, at 701-746-2671, knows the special assessment balance. The Recorder, at 701-780-8262, files the deed after closing.

Ask each office for a figure dated for your closing day, not for today. Penalties step up on fixed dates, so a number that was right in March may be wrong by May. Put the three numbers together and you can see what you will net before you sign anything.

The title company usually does this legwork once a contract exists, but you can start earlier. Gather your latest statement, your mortgage payoff letter and, if you inherited the house, the estate paperwork.

A cash buyer takes the house as it stands. You do not coordinate repairs, hold open houses or wait on a lender's approval. The county steps stay the same: taxes and specials are paid at closing, the Recorder files the deed, and the title company handles the paperwork between them.

What shortens is the calendar. A listing has to find a buyer, then clear inspection requests and loan underwriting. A cash sale skips most of that, which helps when a penalty date or a tax foreclosure date is close. Owners dealing with a tenant move, an estate or a job change often pick it for that reason. Compare the net amount from each route, counting repairs, agent fees and the months of carrying costs, before you decide.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Grand Forks?
faqs.a: The Grand Forks County Treasurer. The city's Assessing Department only values the property.

faqs.q: When is Grand Forks property tax due?
faqs.a: The tax is due January 1 and payable without penalty until March 1. Full payment by February 15 earns a 5 percent discount.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Grand Forks house with unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company pays the taxes and any special assessments from your closing proceeds.

faqs.q: How large was the 1997 flood buyout?
faqs.a: The city bought 850 properties in its voluntary buyout in 1997 and 1998, and 694 dwellings were demolished.

faqs.q: Does North Dakota charge a deed tax on a sale?
faqs.a: No. The state has no deed or mortgage tax, although recording and title fees still apply.
